fields.v: Budanaz, Y. K., Paleari, L., Copik, M., Calotoiu, A., Schneider, T., Choong, B. C. M., Chandran, S., Hulsbergen, L., Widmer, L., Hoefler, T. (2026). HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills. arXiv:2610.20673v1 [cs.SE], 14 Oct 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2610.20673v1 [cs.SE] (IEEE-style layout); no published venue stated
Department of Computer Science, ETH Zurich, Switzerland (nine authors); Institute of High Performance Computing (IHPC), A*STAR, Singapore (Choong); academic / public research

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — benchmarking framework HPCAgent-Bench (689 kernels in three tracks, external judge with hidden fuzzed inputs, intervention-efficacy and weighted-token-cost metrics) evaluated with three open-weight models across eight interventions (skill packets, prompt framings, harnesses), two devices and a second machine

No SDD approach. Interventions on the agent setup (Table XII): Language skill packet (language, OpenMP and method pages plus hints page), Performance Toolkit skill packet (profiling tools; e.g. perfskill.md, papiskill.md), CPF (canonical parallel form as starting source, or CPF page and tool), Git reformulation (kernel posed as a git repository with an issue), Blind (no score tool, one submission), Terse (brief-message instruction), Harness (mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, or AutoKernel add-on in place of Claude Code), RCCL hints skill packet. Control harness Claude Code (version Not stated). Models: Qwen3.8-27B (FP8, SGLang), Kimi-K2.7 (SGLang), OSS-120B (vLLM 0.23.0; 0.27.1 under mini-SWE-agent); default temperature 1

N/A (no SDD approach). Context artefacts used as interventions: Markdown skill packets (language/method pages, profiling-tool pages, RCCL page), a CPF page, a brief-message instruction page. Benchmark artefacts: kernel specified once in NumPy with a YAML manifest (sizes, arrays, difficulty, tuning knobs), generated C/Fortran references and prompt; run config.yaml fixing kernels, language, submission mode, precision, residency and optimizer
N/A (no approach). Episode: one prompt, agent iterates with an optional /score tool (speedup only) and submits one artefact via /submit, graded by the external judge
N/A (autonomous episodes). Flagged answers (roofline, implausibility or static-source checks) go to manual inspection (54 of 10,633 graded answers)
Single artefact — skill packets and instruction pages added to the agent's context as controlled interventions (plus harness swaps), run with agents; no SDD approach
Not classifiable (no specification-driven approach; authors speak of 'skills', 'skill packets' and 'interventions')
Existing code: optimise a given kernel (baseline source and timing driver given; in Git-SciComp posed as a repository with an issue); also write distributed implementations of ML models

Corpus 689 kernels: Loop-Level Reasoning 248, Scientific Computing 171, Machine Learning 270 (levels L1 349, L2 221, L3 119). Experiments: LLR-Focus40 40 kernels, Git-SciComp 10, SciComp35 35, Harness20 20, MLScale 19 models; 10,633 graded answers; budgets 12M-60M tokens and 4-20 h per episode

High-performance computing: loop-level compiler transformations (TSVC-2 and extensions); scientific kernels from weather and climate, electronic structure, plasma physics and fusion, seismology, molecular dynamics and proxy applications (13 Berkeley dwarfs); deep-learning operators and models (mainly from KernelBench)
N/A (no human participants)

Weighted token cost C_w = w_in·T_in + w_cache·T_cache + w_out·T_out with billed (1, 0.1, 1, default), effective (1, 0, 1) and total (1, 1, 1) weights; cost ratio ρC per intervention; token and wall-time budgets per episode; dollar cost deliberately not reported

Success rate R (task solved if every graded fuzzed input is correct within precision-specific tolerances); speedup score (geometric mean of per-input speedups, credited only if a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test gives p < 0.1); parallel efficiency η for strong and weak scaling; intervention efficacy ratios ρR, ρS, ρC with g/l (kernels solved only after/before)
None
None

Portability to a second machine (share skipped for device-specific code, share correct, Spearman rank correlation of per-kernel speedups, geometric-mean gain); run-to-run spread of speedups and implemented optimisations; score-tool calls per task; flagged/cheating attempts

Automatic: external judge service grades correctness on inputs from two secret seeds (score vs submission), times baseline and answer with warmup and n runs over m input draws, returns only a speedup; roofline, implausibility, device and static-source checks flag answers for manual inspection; tokens read from agent transcripts (tokenizer fallback undercounts 2-4%). Statistics: geometric means with 95% log-t intervals, two-sided paired t-tests on log ratios, Benjamini-Hochberg q < 0.05 per panel; solved counts reported, not tested

No success criterion for a configuration is stated; per task, solved = all fuzzed inputs correct, speedup credited only if significant. One episode per kernel per setup (rerun once with 2-4× budget if the limit is hit); most results reported as ratios in figures. Values stated in the text: (a) Claude Code + Qwen3.8-27B / Kimi-K2.7 / OSS-120B, LLR-Focus40 GPU, speedup over CPU Numba HIP vs OpenMP target offloading: 54.5× vs 38.7× / 55.6× vs 32.3× / 21.6× vs 16.6×, 37-40 of 40 solved; agents 2.9-4.2× faster than Pluto (32/40 solved, 1.55×) and 1.8-3.4× faster than PPCG (16 solved, 9.2×). (b) MLScale, 16 GPUs on 4 nodes, over single-GPU PyTorch: Qwen3.8-27B 10.0×, Kimi-K2.7 5.7×, OSS-120B < 1× (PyTorch distributed 3.9×). (c) Interventions vs control: Language skill packet: no significant speedup change except OSS-120B in C (ρS = 0.90); on GPU cost up for OSS-120B 1.5× (HIP) and 2.0× (OpenMP offload), Qwen3.8-27B 1.7× (OpenMP offload). Performance Toolkit: no change in speedup or cost. CPF: Qwen3.8-27B ρC = 2.05 at unchanged speedup; OSS-120B ρS = 1.23 at unchanged cost; Kimi-K2.7 no change. Terse: no significant change, 2-5 fewer kernels solved per setup. Blind: speedup lower in 3 of 8 setups (Kimi-K2.7 C ρS = 0.66; OSS-120B C 0.74, Fortran 0.65); HIP solved 31 vs 39 (Qwen3.8-27B), 29 vs 39 (OSS-120B). Git reformulation: all 10 solved, ρS = 0.52-0.68 and ρC = 0.73-1.43, none significant. Harness20: no harness changes speedup; OpenHands cuts Qwen3.8-27B billed tokens 2.1×, mini-SWE-agent cuts OSS-120B 3.0×; AutoKernel raises OSS-120B cost 1.3× (score calls 5.4 vs 1.8). (d) Portability MI300A → GH200, skipped / correct / rs / gain: C 29% / 99% / 0.96 / 1.61×; Fortran 0% / 93% / 0.92 / 1.40×; HIP 25% / 95% / 0.84 / 1.16×; Triton 4% / 98% / 0.95 / 1.09×. Each configuration: quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors; cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors

Tasks: kernel sets per experiment (Table II, Tables VII-XI). Configurations: paired setups (Table XIII) that share model, language, device and kernels and differ only in one intervention; 3 models; harness Claude Code as default and control. Baselines: Numba (LLR), fastest of auto-parallelised C, sequential C and parallel Numba (SC), PyTorch on one GPU (ML); Pluto and PPCG as comparators. Held constant: model, language, device, skill packets, harness, budget, judge, fixed container images, submission mode per experiment (open- or single-submission). Acceptance tests: hidden fuzzed inputs with numerical tolerances. Repetitions: one episode per kernel per setup; noise study with 20 runs of 3 kernels at temperature 0 and 1. Human intervention: none. Hardware: AMD Instinct MI300A APU; second machine GH200

Across 40 matched setups interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to 3.0×; the token weighting alone changes a cost effect up to threefold (e.g. OpenHands saves Qwen3.8-27B nothing by effective cost, ρC = 1.10, but 3.2× by total cost). Feedback (score tool) matters most for success and speed. Agents beat automatic parallelisers by up to 4.2× and write distributed code that scales (Qwen3.8-27B 10.0× over single-GPU PyTorch). Optimisations transfer: 93-99% of portable answers stay correct on GH200, rs ≥ 0.84. Run-to-run noise is large: on kmp at temperature 1 Qwen3.8-27B speedups span 0.51-100× (temperature 0: 1.8-11×)

Yes, by the authors' account: the framework detected cheating (e.g. a cached-result answer scoring 5,309× on fixed inputs falls to 20× on new draws; GPU use in CPU tests; timing side channel), attributed effects to single interventions with paired statistics, and reproduced rankings on a second machine. Limits stated: one run of one kernel is a single sample of a stochastic agent, so results need enough kernels or repetitions; cost conclusions depend on the stated token weighting; log-t intervals assume normal log-ratios; no intervals below six pairs; tokenizer fallback undercounts tokens 2-4%

No dedicated limitations section. Stated caveats: stochastic agents (speedups on one kernel span two orders of magnitude); token-weighting dependence of cost effects; statistical assumptions; device-specific answers excluded from portability. Gaps in prior benchmarks: narrow device, language or domain coverage; unreliable speedups (agents exploit loopholes and overfit exposed tests); incompatible cost conventions. Answer to the practical question: tested interventions mostly make the agent cheaper rather than better

Framework released (https://github.com/spcl/HPCAgent-Bench) and all material in an anonymised Zenodo archive (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22974128) with every judge observation, token counts and skill-packet versions; one command regenerates every figure and number. No pre-registration. Languages: C, Fortran (CPU); HIP, Triton, OpenMP target offloading, HIP with RCCL (GPU); NumPy specifications, Python interface. AI use statement: generative AI used for framework code, figures, related-work search and drafting, reviewed by the authors. Possible inconsistency: abstract and conclusion say interventions change speedup significantly 'only twice' in 40 setups, while §IV-D reports a significant speedup change for the Language packet (OSS-120B C), CPF (OSS-120B) and Blind in 3 of 8 setups; check which setups form the 40. The CPF intervention comes from the authors' own work [52]

rev.why: Null effects are reported and conclusions mostly follow, but the headline claim (abstract and conclusion: of 40 comparisons only two change speedup significantly) cannot be reconciled from the text with §IV-D, which reports significant speedup changes for the Language packet (OSS-120B C), the CPF (OSS-120B) and Blind in 3 of 8 setups; Table XIII does not show which 40 pairs are counted. If Blind is in the 40, the headline understates the effects and Partly would fit.

fields.warn: O resumo diz que só 2 de 40 comparações mudam a speedup, mas a §IV-D mostra pelo menos 5 (incluindo Blind). Confirma na Tabela XIII/Fig. 3 e 5 quais são as 40 e decide entre Yes e Partly.
